intelligence.human_view: The question was a clock question — which month counts as the first payout month — and his answer dissolves the clock entirely. A clock would have been a rule to administer, a date to argue about, a promise to break the first time the money lands late. "When we get paid, they get paid" is not a policy, it is a fact about how the money moves: the citizen's pay is downstream of ours, and the account shows that honestly — pending while it is pending, official when it is official, paid when it is paid. The three states are the whole interface; there is nothing to explain beyond them. And the restraint matters as much as the rule: no heavy restrictions at the start, protections only if a real problem arrives, and then a plain notification, not a silent change. That is the same shape as the rest of the agreement — trust first, guardrails only where a real problem proves they are needed. The candidate text softened this into "can't promise a payday yet" and labelled the states PENDING / PAID; his settled words win over it, and the merge kept his version inside the candidate base.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you and your friend sell lemonade together. When someone pays you, you share the money with your friend right away! You don't make your friend wait for a special day on the calendar. First the money comes in, then you share it. Simple!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — when the money comes in, everybody gets their share straight away. No waiting for a special date, no complicated rules. Your little account shows what's still coming, what's ready, and what's already paid — clear as day. And we don't pile on fussy rules unless there's a real problem — and if that ever happens, we'll just tell you plainly.
intelligence.naya_view: When we get paid, they get paid. Pending until it's official, official until it's paid — and I say so plainly, in three words on the account, not a calendar of rules.
